title: 6.13 — Restricted Regression and Linear Hypothesis Testing
breadcrumb: Unit VI → Regression and linear models → 6.13 Restricted regression
engineName: Impose linear restrictions on regression coefficients and test them using nested-model F statistics.
objectives: Express restrictions on regression coefficients in the matrix form Rβ=r.
Distinguish unrestricted OLS from restricted least squares.
Calculate a restricted least-squares estimate for a simple linear restriction.
Use the extra sum-of-squares F statistic to test q linear restrictions.
Recognise the equivalence F=t² for a single linear restriction.
Distinguish exact restrictions from stochastic restrictions and explain mixed estimation.

prereq.name: OLS estimation and residual sums of squares
prereq.why: Restricted regression compares the fit of nested unrestricted and restricted models.

prereq.name: Matrix algebra and linear restrictions
prereq.why: The restrictions are represented by Rβ=r and the restricted estimator uses matrix projections.

prereq.name: F tests and degrees of freedom
prereq.why: The joint test uses the number of restrictions and the unrestricted residual degrees of freedom.

traps: A linear restriction has the form Rβ=r, where R has q independent rows.
Restricted least squares minimises RSS subject to the restrictions; its RSS cannot be smaller than unrestricted OLS RSS.
The extra sum-of-squares F statistic is [(RSS_R−RSS_U)/q]/[RSS_U/(n−k)] for q restrictions.
The unrestricted model is nested within the restricted model in the sense that the restriction defines a subset of the parameter space.
For one restriction, the classical F statistic equals the square of the corresponding t statistic.
Exact restrictions impose a fixed equality; stochastic restrictions allow deviations with a specified variance.
Mixed estimation combines sample information with external or prior linear information.
A restriction matrix with redundant rows does not represent q independent restrictions; use its rank.
howto: Write the null restriction as Rβ=r and count independent restrictions q=rank(R). Estimate the unrestricted model, then estimate or calculate the restricted fit. Compare RSS values with the extra sum-of-squares F statistic. For one restriction, check that F=t². If the restriction is stochastic rather than exact, describe the variance of the restriction error and use mixed estimation rather than imposing it as a hard equality.

scenes.title: Refresh OLS fit, hypotheses and degrees of freedom
scenes.objective: Recover the regression tools needed for restricted estimation.
body: Restricted regression asks what happens when the coefficient vector is required to satisfy one or more linear equalities. It compares the constrained fit with unrestricted OLS.
The core quantities are the residual sum of squares, the number of independent restrictions and the residual degrees of freedom.

items.recall: The residual sum of squares over all coefficient vectors.
refresh: OLS chooses coefficients that minimise the sum of squared residuals.
Without restrictions, the parameter vector can take any value allowed by the model design.
A restricted model searches over a smaller set of coefficient vectors, so its minimum RSS cannot be lower.

items.ask: What is a linear hypothesis on β?
items.recall: A linear equation or set of equations involving regression coefficients.
refresh: A single restriction can be β₁=β₂ or β₁+2β₂=3.
Several restrictions can be collected in matrix form Rβ=r.
The number of independent restrictions is the rank of R, not necessarily the number of displayed rows.

items.ask: What are the residual degrees of freedom in a model with n observations and k parameters?
refresh: The unrestricted model estimates k coefficients, including the intercept if present.
The residual degrees of freedom are n−k under the usual full-rank setup.
This quantity appears in the denominator of the classical regression F statistic.

ask.q: Why must restricted RSS be at least as large as unrestricted RSS?
ask.nudge: The restricted coefficient set is a subset of the unrestricted parameter space.

scenes.title: What does a restriction cost?
scenes.objective: Build an intuitive picture of constrained regression.
body: Suppose an unrestricted model estimates two slopes as 2 and 3, but theory suggests their sum should equal 4. The restriction removes coefficient combinations that do not satisfy that equality.

The constrained estimator adjusts the coefficients to satisfy the restriction while minimising the increase in residual error. It is not simply a matter of changing one coefficient and leaving the other fixed.
The F test asks whether the loss of fit from imposing the restriction is large relative to the unexplained variation remaining in the unrestricted model.

scenario.teaser: Theory says two slopes should sum to four
scenario.title: Constrain the coefficient vector
body: A researcher estimates two coefficients with unrestricted OLS and obtains β̂₁=2 and β̂₂=3. A theory proposes that β₁+β₂=4.
The unrestricted estimate does not satisfy the restriction because its sum is five. Restricted least squares chooses the closest coefficient vector in the OLS metric that satisfies the equality.
If the regressors are orthonormal so that X′X=I, the adjustment is shared equally: the restricted estimate becomes (1.5,2.5), which sums to four.
The restriction may improve scientific interpretability, but the F test evaluates whether the increase in RSS is statistically large.
scenario.q: What is the restricted coefficient vector in the orthonormal example?

ask.q: Does imposing a restriction guarantee a smaller RSS?
ask.nudge: Compare the feasible coefficient sets for restricted and unrestricted OLS.

scenes.title: Write restrictions in matrix form
scenes.objective: Represent multiple coefficient restrictions as Rβ=r.

blocks.body: Rβ=r, where β is the k×1 coefficient vector, R is a q×k restriction matrix and r is a q×1 vector. The independent restriction count is q=rank(R).
For β₁+β₂=4 with β=(β₁,β₂)′, R=[1,1] and r=[4]. For β₁=β₂, R=[1,−1] and r=[0].
If one row of R is a linear combination of other rows, it adds no independent restriction. Use rank(R) to determine the numerator degrees of freedom.
The estimator minimises (Y−Xβ)′(Y−Xβ) subject to Rβ=r. It adjusts the unrestricted OLS vector to the nearest feasible vector under the X′X metric.

scenes.title: Test restrictions using the RSS increase
scenes.objective: Apply the extra sum-of-squares F statistic.

blocks.body: F=[(RSS_R−RSS_U)/q]/[RSS_U/(n−k)], where q is the number of independent restrictions and k is the number of unrestricted parameters.
RSS_R−RSS_U measures the additional unexplained variation caused by imposing the restrictions. Divide by q to obtain the average cost per restriction.
RSS_U/(n−k) is the unrestricted residual mean square, the estimated error variance under the unrestricted model.
A large F statistic means the fit deteriorates substantially when the restrictions are imposed. Compare with the F(q,n−k) reference distribution under the classical assumptions.

ask.q: What does a large F statistic say about the restrictions?
ask.nudge: The restricted model loses too much fit relative to the unrestricted residual variation.

scenes.title: Exact restrictions versus uncertain prior information
scenes.objective: Distinguish hard constraints from stochastic restrictions.
body: An exact restriction says the coefficient combination must equal a fixed value, such as β₁+β₂=4. Restricted least squares imposes that equality exactly.

Sometimes the restriction comes from an external study or prior information that is informative but uncertain. Then it is more realistic to model the restriction error as random with a known or specified covariance.

Mixed estimation weights the sample regression and the external information according to their relative precision. A highly precise restriction receives more weight; a noisy restriction receives less.

scenario.title: Do not force uncertain information to be exact
body: A transport study estimates an elasticity near 0.8 but reports a standard error. A new sample regression estimates the same elasticity from a different population.
Treating the external estimate as an exact equality would ignore its uncertainty. A stochastic restriction instead represents the external information as Rβ=r+v, where v has a specified covariance.

Mixed estimation combines the new sample information and the external restriction, weighting each according to its precision. If the external variance is very small, it has more influence; if it is large, the sample data dominate.
The distinction is substantive: exact restrictions are hard constraints, while stochastic restrictions are noisy pieces of information.
scenario.q: Why is a stochastic restriction not imposed as an exact equality?
scenario.answer: Because the external information has uncertainty represented by a random restriction error.

ask.q: What determines the weight given to a stochastic restriction?
ask.nudge: Think about the variance or precision of the external information.

scenes.title: Exam traps: restricted regression
scenes.objective: Avoid common errors in restrictions and F testing.
scenes.intro: Mark each statement true or false.

items.claim: Restricted RSS cannot be smaller than unrestricted RSS.
items.why: Unrestricted OLS minimises RSS over a larger parameter space.

items.claim: The number of restrictions is always the number of displayed equations.
items.why: Redundant restrictions do not add independent information; use rank(R).

items.claim: For one restriction, the classical F statistic equals t squared.
items.why: Both test the same one-dimensional linear hypothesis.

items.claim: The numerator degrees of freedom equal n−k.
items.why: The numerator degrees of freedom equal q; n−k is the denominator degrees of freedom.

items.claim: Stochastic restrictions are imposed as exact equalities.
items.why: They allow a random deviation with specified uncertainty.

scenes.title: Transfer problem: interpret a restriction test
scenes.objective: Explain a joint F test in context.
scenes.problem: A model tests H₀:β₂=β₃=0. The unrestricted model has RSS=100; the restricted model has RSS=112; q=2 and n−k=20. Compute F and state what it measures.
hints: There are two independent zero restrictions.
Use the increase in RSS divided by q.
Divide by the unrestricted residual mean square.
scenes.answer: F=[(112−100)/2]/(100/20)=6/5=1.2. It measures the average fit loss per restriction relative to the unrestricted residual mean square.

solution.say: Compute the unrestricted residual mean square.
Divide numerator mean square by denominator mean square.

ask.q: What does the numerator degree of freedom equal?
ask.nudge: It is the number of independent coefficient restrictions.

scenes.title: Summary: restrict, compare and test
scenes.objective: Compress restricted regression into an exam-ready checklist.
body: Write the hypothesis as Rβ=r and use q=rank(R) independent restrictions. Restricted least squares minimises RSS subject to the equality; its RSS cannot be lower than unrestricted OLS RSS.

The extra sum-of-squares statistic is F=[(RSS_R−RSS_U)/q]/[RSS_U/(n−k)]. The numerator degrees of freedom are q and the denominator degrees of freedom are n−k. For one restriction, F=t² under the classical assumptions.

Exact restrictions are hard equalities. Stochastic restrictions allow deviations with specified uncertainty, and mixed estimation combines the external information with the sample regression according to precision.

ask.q: What are the three steps in a restricted-regression test?
ask.nudge: Write Rβ=r, count q, then compare restricted and unrestricted RSS.

scenes.title: Extension — stochastic restrictions and mixed estimation
scenes.objective: Connect external linear information to a weighted regression problem.

blocks.body: External information can be written Rβ=r+v, where v has mean zero and covariance Ω. Unlike an exact restriction, it allows the coefficient combination to deviate from r.
A common formulation minimises the sample residual sum of squares together with a weighted penalty (Rβ−r)′Ω⁻¹(Rβ−r). The weight is larger when the restriction variance is smaller.
As Ω becomes very small, the stochastic restriction approaches an exact restriction. As Ω becomes very large, the external information receives little weight and the sample regression dominates.

ask.q: What happens when the restriction variance is very small?
ask.nudge: The external information is treated as highly precise.
